title: On Bits and Atoms
subtitle: In 1995, Nicholas Negroponte wrote about “bits versus atoms.” A piece of heterodoxy at the time.
body_html:
In 1995, Nicholas Negroponte wrote about “bits versus atoms.” A piece of heterodoxy at the time. 16 years later, when Peter Thiel’s firm, Founders Found, offered that “we wanted flying cars; instead we got 140 characters,” it was closer to orthodoxy by then. The observation is damning, charged, and apparently consistent with reality. Planes today are slower than they were in the 1960s. We haven’t cured cancer or Alzheimer’s. Where’s the progress? Have we been wasting our time in the world of bits?

Maybe. Code’s scalable, iterable, and low-cost development has long attracted capital and talent. Attention is zero sum, and building a near-zero marginal cost business with powerful network effects is an attractive prospect. Building in the world of atoms is risky and involved. It’s plausible these qualities, and the incentives they produce, have misallocated talent: our best and brightest are optimizing social media algorithms or trading for Jane Street. They could be inventing new materials or curing diseases.

But this supposed dichotomy, between the “real” and digital world, is messy. If only because there is no method of computation that isn’t instantiated physically. But, of course, this objection ignores the spirit of the bits versus atoms observation in favor of its letter. Negroponte, Thiel, and others are pointing out that it feels like a narrow slice of “technology” is being developed, at the expense of everything else. Whether the world of bits exists separately from that of atoms, or as a subset of it, is hardly relevant.

However, ontologies shape perceptions. Taking Negroponte or Thiel’s arguments too literally may lead one to commit themselves to an incoherent distinction, and become blind to progress. Are self-driving cars part of the world of bits or atoms? What about AlphaFold? Real-world assets stored on the Ethereum network?

Reality is continuous. In service of understanding our surroundings and communicating with others, we slice it into various, context-dependent categories. This is a helpful convention. But it is times like our own, when it can be informative to see that when new technologies are created, they interact with other ones. Categories blend, combine, and interact in a massively multi-dimensional fashion. As we embody our artificial intelligence systems, provide them with context, and otherwise integrate these two “worlds,” we will find this debate to be confused and anachronistic.
